Probabilistic forecasting with timestralR

Stefan Janse van Rensburg

Source: vignettes/timestralR.Rmd
timestralR.Rmd

timestralR runs Mistral AI’s Timestral time-series foundation models directly in R. Timestral is a zero-shot forecaster: it is pretrained on a large corpus of time series, so you give it a context (the history you have) and a horizon, and it returns a full predictive distribution without any fitting. Every forecast has 21 quantiles per step, from the 1% to the 99% level.

The package has no Python or PyTorch dependency. The official safetensors checkpoints are downloaded once, and the transformer runs natively on R’s BLAS.

This vignette covers the whole interface:

  1. loading a model and making a first forecast;
  2. working with the forecast: quantiles, data frames and plots;
  3. multivariate series and batches of series;
  4. missing values and observation masks;
  5. numeric and categorical covariates;
  6. time indexes from ts, zoo and xts;
  7. the tidyverts (tsibble input and output, fable integration) and the forecast package;
  8. evaluating forecasts: scoring and rolling-origin backtests;
  9. options, backends, and using the package in parallel code.
library(timestralR)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")))

1. Loading a model

Checkpoints come in four sizes: "5M", "28M", "123M" and "209M". They range from 21 MB to 837 MB on disk. timestral_load() downloads a checkpoint to a per-user cache on first use; afterwards it loads from disk. A local directory holding config.json and model.safetensors also works, as does any Hugging Face repository ID ("owner/name") that holds a Timestral checkpoint, such as a fine-tuned model.

m <- timestral_load("28M")
m
#> <timestral_model> 49b26409ac87b5935539a5d8ffe7f397b720db47  d_model = 384  layers = 12  max_context = 32768 
#>   covariates: past and known-future

The printout also says which covariates the checkpoint can condition on; timestral_supports_covariates() and timestral_supports_known_covariates() return the same as TRUE or FALSE, which is useful when code receives a checkpoint it did not choose. Every official checkpoint forecasts the same 21 quantile levels (another checkpoint’s own levels are in each forecast’s fc$levels):

timestral_levels()
#>  [1] 0.01 0.05 0.10 0.15 0.20 0.25 0.30 0.35 0.40 0.45 0.50 0.55 0.60 0.65 0.70
#> [16] 0.75 0.80 0.85 0.90 0.95 0.99

2. A first forecast

timestral_forecast() takes a model, a series y, and a horizon h. Here we forecast three years of the classic airline passengers series.

fc <- timestral_forecast(m, AirPassengers, h = 36)
fc
#> <timestral_forecast> 1 variate(s), h = 36, 21 quantiles
#>     med
#> 1 447.3
#> 2 416.7
#> 3 469.4
#> 4 480.4
#> 5 496.5
#> 6 576.1

predict(m, AirPassengers, h = 36) is the same call through R’s predict() generic. Timestral is zero-shot, so there is no fitted model to predict from: the series itself is the newdata.

The plot() method draws a fan chart: the observed history, the median forecast, and nested 50%, 80%, 90% and 98% central intervals.

plot(fc, main = "AirPassengers: 36-month Timestral forecast",
     ylab = "Passengers (thousands)")
Base-graphics fan chart from plot(): history, median and nested central intervals.

Extracting results

The full forecast is a (variate, step, level) array in fc$quantiles. The accessors return single levels; because the input was a ts, they return a ts that starts right after the data.

dim(fc$quantiles)
#> [1]  1 36 21
window(timestral_median(fc), end = c(1961, 6))
#>        Jan   Feb   Mar   Apr   May   Jun
#> 1961 447.3 416.7 469.4 480.4 496.5 576.1
window(timestral_quantile(fc, 0.9), end = c(1961, 6))
#>        Jan   Feb   Mar   Apr   May   Jun
#> 1961 465.2 439.3 494.0 506.9 525.3 608.9

as_forecast_df() gives a tidy long data frame with one column per quantile level and the forecast time:

head(as_forecast_df(fc)[, c("variate", "step", "time", "q10", "q50", "q90")])
#>   variate step time   q10   q50   q90
#> 1      V1    1 1961 430.6 447.3 465.2
#> 2      V1    2 1961 395.6 416.7 439.3
#> 3      V1    3 1961 446.4 469.4 494.0
#> 4      V1    4 1961 454.9 480.4 506.9
#> 5      V1    5 1961 469.4 496.5 525.3
#> 6      V1    6 1961 547.4 576.1 608.9

ggplot2

When ggplot2 is installed, autoplot() draws the same fan chart as a ggplot object, so the usual ggplot2 modifications apply.

autoplot(fc) +
  labs(title = "AirPassengers", y = "Passengers (thousands)")
The same forecast with autoplot().

autolayer() adds only the forecast bands and median to an existing plot. A natural use is a backtest. Hold out the last three years, forecast them, and overlay what actually happened:

train <- window(AirPassengers, end = c(1957, 12))
test  <- window(AirPassengers, start = c(1958, 1))
fc_bt <- timestral_forecast(m, train, h = length(test))

actual <- data.frame(time = as.numeric(time(AirPassengers)),
                     value = as.numeric(AirPassengers),
                     part = ifelse(time(AirPassengers) < 1958,
                                   "training data", "held out"))
ggplot(actual, aes(time, value)) +
  autolayer(fc_bt) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = part), linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("training data" = "black",
                                 "held out" = "#D55E00"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Backtest: forecasting 1958-1960 from data up to 1957",
       x = NULL, y = "Passengers (thousands)")
Backtest: the 1958-1960 forecast from data up to 1957, with the held-out values in orange.

How well calibrated are the intervals here? The share of held-out months inside each central interval:

q <- fc_bt$quantiles[1, , ]
lv <- fc_bt$levels
inside <- function(p) {
  lo <- q[, which.min(abs(lv - (1 - p) / 2))]
  hi <- q[, which.min(abs(lv - (1 + p) / 2))]
  mean(test >= lo & test <= hi)
}
data.frame(interval = c("50%", "80%", "90%", "98%"),
           coverage = sapply(c(0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.98), inside))
#>   interval coverage
#> 1      50%   0.5000
#> 2      80%   0.8333
#> 3      90%   0.9722
#> 4      98%   1.0000

3. Multivariate series and batches

Variates of one series are forecast jointly: the model attends across them, so related series can inform each other. Pass a matrix, data frame or mts with one column per variate.

deaths <- cbind(male = mdeaths, female = fdeaths)
fc_mv <- timestral_forecast(m, deaths, h = 24)
dim(fc_mv$quantiles)
#> [1]  2 24 21
autoplot(fc_mv) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Purples", name = "Interval") +  # restyle bands
  labs(title = "UK lung disease deaths, forecast jointly", y = "Deaths")
Two variates forecast jointly; autoplot() facets by variate.

Batches are independent series forecast in one call. Pass a list of series (or a 3-D array). The series must have the same length, and the result gains a leading series dimension. A time index shared by every series in the list is kept.

batch <- list(total = ldeaths, male = mdeaths, female = fdeaths)
fc_b <- timestral_forecast(m, batch, h = 24)
dim(fc_b$quantiles)
#> [1]  3  1 24 21
dimnames(fc_b$quantiles)$series
#> [1] "total"  "male"   "female"

plots <- lapply(seq_along(batch), function(i)
  autoplot(fc_b, series = i) +
    labs(subtitle = names(batch)[i], x = NULL, y = NULL))
wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 1, guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(title = "A batch of three series in one call") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Three independent series forecast in a single batched call.

Batching is faster than looping because the series share every matrix product. Each series is still forecast independently: the results match one-at-a-time forecasts.

fc_one <- timestral_forecast(m, mdeaths, h = 24)
max(abs(fc_b$quantiles["male", 1, , ] - fc_one$quantiles[1, , ]))
#> [1] 6.821e-12

4. Missing values and observation masks

NA values in y are treated as missing, so no imputation is needed. Below, a whole year of the passengers series is lost:

ap_gap <- AirPassengers
window(ap_gap, start = c(1955, 1), end = c(1955, 12)) <- NA
fc_gap <- timestral_forecast(m, ap_gap, h = 36)
autoplot(fc_gap) +
  labs(title = "A year of missing data in the context",
       y = "Passengers (thousands)")
Forecasting through a year of missing values in the context.

An observation_mask (logical, shaped like y) marks extra values as missing without editing the data. This is useful for excluding known anomalies. Here a data-entry error multiplies one month by ten. Masking that month removes its influence on the forecast:

ap_bad <- AirPassengers
ap_bad[length(ap_bad) - 3] <- 10 * ap_bad[length(ap_bad) - 3]
mask <- rep(TRUE, length(ap_bad))
mask[length(ap_bad) - 3] <- FALSE

fc_raw    <- timestral_forecast(m, ap_bad, h = 24)
fc_masked <- timestral_forecast(m, ap_bad, h = 24, observation_mask = mask)

lims <- c(0, 1500)
(autoplot(fc_raw) + coord_cartesian(ylim = lims) +
   labs(subtitle = "outlier used")) +
(autoplot(fc_masked) + coord_cartesian(ylim = lims) +
   labs(subtitle = "outlier masked")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
An outlier left in the context (left) and masked with observation_mask (right).

5. Covariates

Timestral can condition on covariates of three kinds:

  • past_covariates: known over the context only (T rows), such as a leading indicator that has no forecast;
  • known_covariates: known over the context and the horizon (T + h rows), such as planned promotions, prices or holidays;
  • categorical_past_covariates and categorical_known_covariates: integer category codes (weekday, store type, …), target-encoded internally.

Covariates are passed with time in rows, one column per covariate. As an example, here are simulated daily sales of a product with a weekly pattern and occasional promotions that lift sales by about 60%. The promotion calendar is planned, so it is also known for the 8 weeks we want to forecast.

n_ctx <- 364; h <- 56; n <- n_ctx + h
day <- seq_len(n)
weekday <- (day - 1) %% 7                       # 0 = Monday
promo <- as.numeric(runif(n) < 0.12)
promo[n_ctx + c(5, 6, 19, 20, 33, 34, 47, 48)] <- 1  # planned promotions
base <- 100 + 0.05 * day + c(0, -5, -5, 0, 10, 25, 15)[weekday + 1]
sales <- base * (1 + 0.6 * promo) * exp(rnorm(n, sd = 0.05))

y_ctx <- sales[seq_len(n_ctx)]
ggplot(data.frame(day = day, sales = sales, promo = factor(promo)),
       aes(day, sales)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = promo), size = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n_ctx + 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0" = "grey40", "1" = "#D55E00"),
                      labels = c("regular day", "promotion"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Simulated daily sales; the dashed line ends the context",
       x = "Day", y = "Sales")
Simulated daily sales with weekly seasonality and promotion spikes.

Without covariates the model sees the spikes in the history but cannot know when the next ones will happen. Passing the promotion calendar as a known covariate, and the weekday as a categorical known covariate, lets it place them:

fc_plain <- timestral_forecast(m, y_ctx, h = h)
fc_cov <- timestral_forecast(
  m, y_ctx, h = h,
  known_covariates = cbind(promo = promo),
  categorical_known_covariates = cbind(weekday = weekday)
)
cov_panel <- function(f, title) {
  qs <- f$quantiles[1, , ]
  d <- data.frame(day = n_ctx + seq_len(h), actual = sales[n_ctx + seq_len(h)],
                  lo = qs[, "0.10"], hi = qs[, "0.90"], med = qs[, "0.50"])
  hist <- data.frame(day = (n_ctx - 55):n_ctx, sales = y_ctx[(n_ctx - 55):n_ctx])
  ggplot(d, aes(day)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#6BAED6", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(data = hist, aes(day, sales), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_line(aes(y = med), colour = "#08519C", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(aes(y = actual), colour = "#D55E00", size = 0.9) +
    labs(subtitle = title, x = "Day", y = "Sales")
}
cov_panel(fc_plain, "no covariates") /
  cov_panel(fc_cov, "promotion calendar + weekday as known covariates") +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Median and 80% interval; dots are the held-out actuals")
The same horizon without covariates (top) and with the promotion calendar and weekday as known covariates (bottom).

A simple score shows the gain, using the mean absolute error of the median and the mean pinball (quantile) loss over all 21 levels:

actual <- sales[n_ctx + seq_len(h)]
pinball <- function(f) {
  qs <- f$quantiles[1, , ]
  mean(sapply(seq_along(f$levels), function(j) {
    e <- actual - qs[, j]
    mean(pmax(f$levels[j] * e, (f$levels[j] - 1) * e))
  }))
}
data.frame(
  model = c("no covariates", "with covariates"),
  MAE = c(mean(abs(actual - fc_plain$quantiles[1, , "0.50"])),
          mean(abs(actual - fc_cov$quantiles[1, , "0.50"]))),
  pinball = c(pinball(fc_plain), pinball(fc_cov))
)
#>             model    MAE pinball
#> 1   no covariates 21.483   7.613
#> 2 with covariates  7.586   2.634

Past-only covariates use the same row layout over the context only, for example past_covariates = cbind(footfall = footfall[1:n_ctx]). For a batch, give a list with one covariate matrix per series.

6. Time indexes: ts, zoo and xts

A ts input keeps its time attributes, as above. zoo and xts inputs keep their index (Dates, POSIXct, …). The forecast stores a future_index that extends the last observed interval, and as_forecast_df() reports real dates.

library(zoo)
dates <- as.Date("2024-01-01") + seq_len(n) - 1
sales_z <- zoo(sales, order.by = dates)
fc_z <- timestral_forecast(m, sales_z[seq_len(n_ctx)], h = 14)
head(as_forecast_df(fc_z)[, c("time", "q10", "q50", "q90")], 4)
#>         time   q10   q50   q90
#> 1 2024-12-30 109.3 123.6 146.8
#> 2 2024-12-31 104.8 109.9 124.7
#> 3 2025-01-01 105.9 112.8 135.9
#> 4 2025-01-02 107.9 118.9 147.3

When y and a covariate both carry a time index, the indexes must line up. This catches off-by-one and misaligned joins early:

promo_z <- zoo(cbind(promo = promo), order.by = dates + 1)  # shifted a day
tryCatch(
  timestral_forecast(m, sales_z[seq_len(n_ctx)], h = 14,
                     known_covariates = promo_z[seq_len(n_ctx + 14)]),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> [1] "known_covariates time index does not align with the time index of y"

7. The tidyverts

tsibble input and output

A tsibble can be passed directly. Keys become the batch and measured variables become jointly forecast variates. Rows are put in index order, and implicit gaps in a regular tsibble are filled with missing values. Here are quarterly holiday trips to four Australian states:

library(tsibble)
library(dplyr)
holidays <- tourism |>
  filter(Purpose == "Holiday",
         State %in% c("New South Wales", "Victoria",
                      "Queensland", "Western Australia")) |>
  group_by(State) |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips)) |>
  ungroup()
holidays
#> # A tsibble: 320 x 3 [1Q]
#> # Key:       State [4]
#>    State           Quarter Trips
#>    <chr>             <qtr> <dbl>
#>  1 New South Wales 1998 Q1 4033.
#>  2 New South Wales 1998 Q2 3262.
#>  3 New South Wales 1998 Q3 2681.
#>  4 New South Wales 1998 Q4 3083.
#>  5 New South Wales 1999 Q1 3635.
#>  6 New South Wales 1999 Q2 2958.
#>  7 New South Wales 1999 Q3 2768.
#>  8 New South Wales 1999 Q4 3121.
#>  9 New South Wales 2000 Q1 3548.
#> 10 New South Wales 2000 Q2 2840.
#> # ℹ 310 more rows
fc_ts <- timestral_forecast(m, holidays, h = 12)
dim(fc_ts$quantiles)          # series x variate x step x level
#> [1]  4  1 12 21
as_tsibble(fc_ts) |> select(series, Quarter, q10, q50, q90)
#> # A tsibble: 48 x 5 [1Q]
#> # Key:       series [4]
#>    series          Quarter   q10   q50   q90
#>    <chr>             <qtr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 New South Wales 2018 Q1 3472. 3738. 4030.
#>  2 New South Wales 2018 Q2 2962. 3237. 3545.
#>  3 New South Wales 2018 Q3 2921. 3207. 3505.
#>  4 New South Wales 2018 Q4 2987. 3297. 3606.
#>  5 New South Wales 2019 Q1 3394. 3750. 4097.
#>  6 New South Wales 2019 Q2 2952. 3287. 3638.
#>  7 New South Wales 2019 Q3 2905. 3259. 3621.
#>  8 New South Wales 2019 Q4 2988. 3350. 3719.
#>  9 New South Wales 2020 Q1 3357. 3795. 4223.
#> 10 New South Wales 2020 Q2 2931. 3336. 3755.
#> # ℹ 38 more rows

as_tsibble() keeps the input’s index name and class (here yearquarter), so forecasts join directly with the observed data. For ts input, the index gets the same class that tsibble::as_tsibble() gives the ts (yearmonth, yearquarter, …).

fc_long <- as_tsibble(fc_ts) |> as_tibble() |> rename(State = series)
recent <- holidays |> filter(Quarter >= yearquarter("2010 Q1"))
ggplot(mapping = aes(Quarter)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_long, aes(ymin = q01, ymax = q99), fill = "#DCE9F3") +
  geom_ribbon(data = fc_long, aes(ymin = q10, ymax = q90), fill = "#8FB6D2") +
  geom_line(data = recent, aes(y = Trips), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = fc_long, aes(y = q50), colour = "#173F5F", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~State, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Holiday trips by state: median, 80% and 98% intervals",
       x = NULL, y = "Trips (thousands)")
Forecasts from a keyed tsibble: one series per state.

as_fable() converts a forecast to a fable whose distribution column holds the 21-quantile distribution, so fable tooling such as hilo(), accuracy() and autoplot() applies:

library(fabletools)
fbl <- as_fable(fc_ts)
fbl
#> # A fable: 48 x 3 [1Q]
#> # Key:     series [4]
#>    series          Quarter        Trips
#>    <chr>             <qtr>       <dist>
#>  1 New South Wales 2018 Q1 quantile[21]
#>  2 New South Wales 2018 Q2 quantile[21]
#>  3 New South Wales 2018 Q3 quantile[21]
#>  4 New South Wales 2018 Q4 quantile[21]
#>  5 New South Wales 2019 Q1 quantile[21]
#>  6 New South Wales 2019 Q2 quantile[21]
#>  7 New South Wales 2019 Q3 quantile[21]
#>  8 New South Wales 2019 Q4 quantile[21]
#>  9 New South Wales 2020 Q1 quantile[21]
#> 10 New South Wales 2020 Q2 quantile[21]
#> # ℹ 38 more rows
fbl |> filter(series == "Victoria") |> hilo(80) |> head(4)
#> # A tsibble: 4 x 4 [1Q]
#> # Key:       series [1]
#>   series   Quarter        Trips          `80%`
#>   <chr>      <qtr>       <dist>         <hilo>
#> 1 Victoria 2018 Q1 quantile[21] [3391, 4102]80
#> 2 Victoria 2018 Q2 quantile[21] [2366, 2899]80
#> 3 Victoria 2018 Q3 quantile[21] [2102, 2544]80
#> 4 Victoria 2018 Q4 quantile[21] [2506, 3149]80

Timestral as a fable model

TIMESTRAL() is a model definition for fabletools::model(). It sits alongside ETS, ARIMA and the rest, and it works with fable’s cross-key machinery, forecasting and accuracy tools. The response is univariate; each key gets its own context. Here we hold out the last three years, fit three models per state, and compare them.

library(fable)
train_tb <- holidays |> filter(Quarter <= yearquarter("2014 Q4"))
test_tb  <- holidays |> filter(Quarter >  yearquarter("2014 Q4"))

fit <- train_tb |>
  model(
    Timestral = TIMESTRAL(Trips, model = m),
    ETS       = ETS(Trips),
    ARIMA     = ARIMA(Trips)
  )
fit
#> # A mable: 4 x 4
#> # Key:     State [4]
#>   State               Timestral          ETS                             ARIMA
#>   <chr>                 <model>      <model>                           <model>
#> 1 New South Wales   <TIMESTRAL> <ETS(A,N,A)> <ARIMA(0,0,0)(0,1,1)[4] w/ drift>
#> 2 Queensland        <TIMESTRAL> <ETS(A,N,A)>  <ARIMA(0,0,0)(1,0,0)[4] w/ mean>
#> 3 Victoria          <TIMESTRAL> <ETS(M,N,M)>          <ARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1)[4]>
#> 4 Western Australia <TIMESTRAL> <ETS(M,N,A)>          <ARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1)[4]>
fc_fbl <- fit |> forecast(h = "3 years")
library(ggtime)   # fable's plotting methods live in ggtime
fc_fbl |>
  autoplot(holidays |> filter(Quarter >= yearquarter("2011 Q1")),
           level = c(80, 95)) +
  facet_grid(State ~ .model, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1", aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  guides(colour = "none", fill = "none") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(size = 7)) +
  labs(title = "Three years ahead: Timestral, ETS and ARIMA (80% and 95% intervals)",
       x = NULL, y = "Trips (thousands)")
Timestral alongside ETS and ARIMA as fable models.

Because the forecasts are proper distributions, fable’s accuracy measures, including the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), evaluate the whole predictive distribution:

fc_fbl |>
  accuracy(holidays, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MASE = MASE,
                                     CRPS = CRPS)) |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(across(c(RMSE, MASE, CRPS), mean)) |>
  arrange(CRPS)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   .model     RMSE  MASE  CRPS
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 ETS        247.  1.51  151.
#> 2 Timestral  260.  1.64  159.
#> 3 ARIMA      288.  1.76  178.

Fitted models store a small handle to the checkpoint, not the weights. A mable therefore stays small when saved with saveRDS(), and it keeps working in a new R session or a parallel worker; the checkpoint is reloaded from disk when needed. The whole mable, with its three models for four states and the training data, is a fraction of the size of the weights:

c(mable_MB   = length(serialize(fit, NULL)) / 1e6,
  weights_MB = file.size(file.path(m$dir, "model.safetensors")) / 1e6)
#>   mable_MB weights_MB 
#>      1.255    111.296

The forecast package

The forecast package has its own forecast() generic, and calling it with a Timestral model returns a "forecast" object, so accuracy(), autoplot() and the rest of that package’s tools work as for ETS or ARIMA. (timestral_as_forecast() converts a forecast you already have.) The intervals come straight from the quantile knots, which are not interpolated, so each level must pair two knots: the default is 80% and 98%, because the 21 knots have no 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles for the usual 95%.

ap_train <- window(AirPassengers, end = c(1957, 12))
ap_test  <- window(AirPassengers, start = c(1958, 1))
fo <- forecast::forecast(m, ap_train, h = 36)
forecast::accuracy(fo, ap_test)
#>                  ME  RMSE   MAE    MPE  MAPE   MASE ACF1 Theil's U
#> Training set    NaN   NaN   NaN    NaN   NaN    NaN   NA        NA
#> Test set     -6.498 17.24 14.54 -2.006 3.583 0.4755 0.49    0.3932

The training-set row is empty because a zero-shot model is not fitted to the context, so there are no in-sample fitted values.

autoplot(fo) +
  autolayer(ap_test, series = "held out") +
  labs(title = "Timestral via forecast::forecast() (80% and 98% intervals)",
       x = NULL, y = "Passengers (thousands)", colour = NULL)
A Timestral forecast as a forecast-package object, with the held-out data.

8. Evaluating forecasts

timestral_score() scores a forecast against the values that were later observed, one row per step. Besides the absolute error of the median (ae) it reports two scores of the whole predictive distribution: the pinball (quantile) loss averaged over the 21 levels (pinball), and an approximation of the continuous ranked probability score (crps). It also reports whether each step fell inside the 80% and 98% intervals. Lower scores are better, and for a point forecast both distribution scores reduce to (about) the absolute error. Here is the section 2 backtest, scored:

sc <- timestral_score(fc_bt, test)
head(sc, 3)
#>   series variate step actual median pinball   crps     ae cover80 cover98
#> 1     S1      V1    1    340  346.2    3.67  3.808  6.178    TRUE    TRUE
#> 2     S1      V1    2    318  334.0   10.13 10.583 15.986   FALSE    TRUE
#> 3     S1      V1    3    362  384.0   14.83 15.501 22.045   FALSE    TRUE
colMeans(sc[, c("ae", "pinball", "crps", "cover80", "cover98")])
#>      ae pinball    crps cover80 cover98 
#> 14.5363 10.6317 11.0107  0.8333  1.0000

One held-out window says little. timestral_backtest() repeats the forecast from several origins, each time using only the data up to the origin, and scores every forecast. Here the origin moves forward a year at a time over the last six years of AirPassengers, with a 12-month horizon each time:

bt <- timestral_backtest(m, AirPassengers, h = 12,
                         origins = seq(72, 132, by = 12))
head(bt[, c("origin", "step", "t", "actual", "median", "crps")], 3)
#>   origin step  t actual median  crps
#> 1     72    1 73    242  230.4 7.265
#> 2     72    2 74    233  226.3 4.197
#> 3     72    3 75    267  265.6 3.259
aggregate(cbind(ae, crps, cover80, cover98) ~ origin, data = bt, FUN = mean)
#>   origin     ae   crps cover80 cover98
#> 1     72 20.257 13.617  0.5833       1
#> 2     84 10.400  7.721  1.0000       1
#> 3     96 12.621  8.757  0.9167       1
#> 4    108 20.281 13.796  0.5000       1
#> 5    120 28.069 18.242  0.5000       1
#> 6    132  9.231  8.027  0.9167       1

Averaging by forecast step shows how accuracy falls off with the horizon:

by_step <- aggregate(cbind(ae, crps) ~ step, data = bt, FUN = mean)
ggplot(rbind(data.frame(step = by_step$step, score = "absolute error",
                        value = by_step$ae),
             data.frame(step = by_step$step, score = "CRPS",
                        value = by_step$crps)),
       aes(step, value, colour = score)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(title = "Backtest accuracy by forecast step", x = "Months ahead",
       y = "Mean score (thousands)", colour = NULL)
Mean CRPS and absolute error by forecast step over six yearly origins.

Covariates and observation_mask are passed over the whole series and cut to each origin: past-only covariates and the mask to the context, known-future covariates to the context plus the horizon. A list of equal-length series is backtested as a batch at each origin. The backtest runs one origin after another; to spread origins over cores, split them and run one backtest per chunk (see ?timestral_backtest and the next section). For tsibbles, the fable route covers the same ground: tsibble::stretch_tsibble(), the TIMESTRAL() model and accuracy().

9. Options, backends and parallel use

The main options of timestral_forecast():

  • symmetric = TRUE (default) averages the forecast with that of the mirrored series (-y), which removes sign bias;
  • clip_nonnegative = TRUE (default) clips quantiles at zero when every observed value is non-negative.

timestral_load() controls the decoding:

  • max_context caps the context length (the default is the trained context length);
  • per_shot_horizon_patches sets how many 32-step patches are decoded per block before the median is fed back for long horizons;
  • quantile_real_cap_k and extreme_value_threshold are safety clamps for extreme inputs.

Backends

The default "native" backend runs the transformer in compiled RcppEigen code. backend = "R" uses the pure-R reference implementation, which is slower but easy to read and step through. The two agree to floating-point precision:

m_R <- timestral_load("28M", backend = "R")
f1 <- timestral_forecast(m, AirPassengers, h = 36)
f2 <- timestral_forecast(m_R, AirPassengers, h = 36)
max(abs(f1$quantiles - f2$quantiles))
#> [1] 1.137e-12

# median time in seconds over three runs
timing <- function(model) median(replicate(3, system.time(
  timestral_forecast(model, AirPassengers, h = 36))[["elapsed"]]))
c(native = timing(m), R = timing(m_R))
#> native      R 
#>  0.059  0.091

Parallel use

The native code is deliberately single-threaded: no OpenMP, no thread pools, and no changes to BLAS threading. Parallelise at the R level instead (parallel, future, mirai, …), with one model per worker. For many series of the same length, batching (section 3) is usually the faster option; for a long backtest, split the origins between workers.

library(parallel)
series <- split(holidays$Trips, holidays$State)
fcs <- mclapply(series, function(y) {
  m <- timestral_load("28M")   # cached on disk; cheap to load
  timestral_forecast(m, y, h = 12)
}, mc.cores = 4)
